title: Put a dropped bicycle chain back on its chainring
instruction: Put the dropped chain back on the chainring, then turn the crank backwards through one full revolution without the chain dropping or jamming.
setup: A full-size bicycle is held upright in a bench repair stand. It has a 40-tooth chainring, 16-tooth rear sprocket, 12-tooth spring tensioner and a linked steel chain at 12.7 mm pitch. The chain hangs off the front chainring and remains on the rear sprocket. The raised stand leaves access below the loose loop. Both robot grippers have silicone pad covers. Restore the photographed drop, crank and stand positions.
scoring: 1.0 if the chain is seated on both sprockets and the crank turns backwards through one full revolution while the chain advances continuously with the chain-feeding hand released and clear, followed by three seconds released without dropping or jamming. 0.5 for half a revolution; 0.25 for a quarter revolution. Otherwise 0. Turning the crank without advancing the chain earns no credit. A broken link or damaged drivetrain scores 0. Judge sprocket engagement and rotation in the video.
fidelity: Rigid native chain links, teeth and revolute pins model contact engagement. A passive spring-loaded idler takes up slack; the steel chain does not stretch. Link side-play, friction and tensioner response are approximate. The robot moves the chain and crank only through contact; no link is snapped onto a tooth or attached to a hand. Development validation is incomplete.
scores: Development diagnostics only; no validated full-score demonstration or Dream baseline yet.
context: Recovering a dropped chain requires feeding flexible linked material onto teeth and checking that the drivetrain runs.
